title: The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups: why startups fail to make something users want
summary: Graham argues there is really one cause of startup death: not making something users want. He lists 18 controllable mistakes that feed into it, from single founders and derivative ideas to slow launches, bad fundraising and half-hearted effort. The deepest cause he names is not trying hard enough.

principles.text: Nearly all startup failure funnels through one mistake: not making something users want.
principles.quote: In a sense there's just one mistake that kills startups: not making something users want. If you make something users want, you'll probably be fine, whatever else you do or don't do.

principles.text: Look for problems, ideally ones you have yourself, rather than imitating existing companies.
principles.quote: Instead of starting from companies and working back to the problems they solved, look for problems and imagine the company that might solve them.

principles.text: Launch something quickly: it forces you to finish work and to learn from real users.
principles.quote: The other reason you need to launch is that it's only by bouncing your idea off users that you fully understand it.

principles.text: Launch a core that is useful on its own and can grow into the whole product.
principles.quote: identify a core that's both (a) useful on its own and (b) something that can be incrementally expanded into the whole project, and then get that done as soon as possible.

principles.text: Solve for value creation first and leave the business model for later; users come before profit.
principles.quote: It is irresponsible not to think about business models. It's just ten times more irresponsible not to think about the product.

principles.text: The biggest mistake is not trying hard enough; most startups fail because founders don't go all in.
principles.quote: Most startups fail because they don't make something people want, and the reason most don't is that they don't try hard enough.
